title: Impressing vintage lace in clay
subtitle: Using fabric lace and doilies to transfer delicate patterns onto a clay slab
excerpt: Pressing lace or a doily into a clay slab and lifting it away leaves the fabric's pattern as a shallow relief in the clay surface. The technique works on any air-dry slab piece and requires no specialist tools. The depth of the impression and the detail depend on the lace weave and how firmly you press.
sourceNotes: Lace impression technique derived from first principles.

glossaryTerms.definition: A flat, even sheet of clay rolled to a consistent thickness
The stage at which clay holds its shape and fine impressed detail without smearing

content.text: Pressing lace into a fresh clay
slab

transfers the fabric's open weave directly onto the clay surface. The approach suits flat tiles, drape-moulded dishes, and pinch pot surfaces. Cotton and linen lace with an open, repeating weave give the clearest prints. Fine silk or closed-weave fabric leaves too little pattern; foam-backed lace does not transfer at all.
What you need
Air-dry clay, about 300 g per tile or dish
Lace or doily (cotton or linen preferred; the more open the weave, the clearer the print)
Pottery rolling pin and slab guides (or two 6 mm-thick wooden dowels) to roll an even slab
Fettling knife or clay cutter for trimming
A smooth work surface (canvas or baking parchment works well and prevents the slab from sticking)
Step-by-step
Roll the clay to 6 mm thickness using slab guides. The clay should be soft but not sticky. If it sticks to the rolling pin, dust the pin lightly with cornflour.
Lay the lace flat onto the slab surface without stretching it. Any tension in the lace will distort when you press and lift.
Roll over the lace with firm, even pressure using the rolling pin. Aim to press the lace about 1-2 mm into the clay surface. Go over the whole area at least twice.
Peel the lace back slowly from one corner. Pull it back on itself at a 45-degree angle rather than lifting straight up. Straight-up lifting pulls clay fibres and blurs the impression.
Cut the tile or dish shape around the impressed area using a fettling knife. Smooth the cut edges with a damp finger.
Allow to dry to leather-hard on a flat, porous surface such as a wooden board or a sheet of newspaper. The clay should lift away from the surface cleanly without sticking or warping.
What a good impression looks like
A clean impression shows the lace weave as a consistent shallow relief across the whole slab. Individual thread impressions are visible. At
leather-hard
stage the pattern is even more defined as the clay surface firms up around the impressed lines.
Common mistakes
Clay too stiff. Clay that has started to dry before rolling resists impression and springs back. Work with fresh, soft clay.
Lace shifts during pressing. Hold one edge down with a finger or use a light spray of water to help the lace sit flat before rolling.
Lifting too quickly. Pulling the lace up sharply smears the impression. Slow, angled peeling gives a clean release.
Painting over the impression before the clay is bone-dry. Wet paint applied to damp clay can fill and blur fine detail. Allow full drying before adding paint or sealant.
